transcript.text: Bosch induction hob PUE611BB1E making a loud buzzing/humming noise when I put my big stockpot on high. Is it about to break?

It is unlikely to be about to break; induction hobs often hum or buzz loudly at high power, especially with heavy stockpots, as the magnetic field interacts with the pan base. This is usually normal behaviour rather than a sign of imminent failure. However, if you are worried it could be an electrical fault, we can quickly rule that out. Please switch off and unplug the hob (or isolate at the consumer unit) for ten minutes to let any residual heat or electronics settle, then try using the pot again. If the noise returns only on high power with no other issues like tripping or burning smells, it is almost certainly just normal induction operation.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
Ok, I can do that. No burning smells or tripping, it just hums on high with the new pot. Should I still unplug it for ten minutes first?

No need to unplug it if there are no burning smells or tripping issues, as the noise is likely just normal induction operation with your heavy stockpot. Induction hobs often hum loudly at high power because of the magnetic field interacting with the pan base. Since you have already confirmed there are no other symptoms like tripping or odours, this points strongly to it being a standard characteristic rather than a fault. To be absolutely sure, try using a different, lighter pan on the same zone; if the noise is much quieter or gone, then your stockpot is simply causing normal induction hum.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
Ok, I tried my heavy cast iron pot on the same zone and that one is quiet. A cheap frying pan I have is noisy too though. So it seems to be the pan rather than the hob?

That suggests it is almost certainly normal induction behaviour rather than a fault with your hob. Induction hobs work by creating a magnetic field, and some pan materials or base designs can vibrate at high power levels, causing that humming sound. Since the heavy cast iron pot was quiet but the cheap frying pan was noisy, it suggests the noise depends on how the specific pan interacts with the magnetic field. You do not need to worry about your hob breaking; this is a common characteristic of induction cooking. If you prefer less noise, you might find that using heavier or thicker-bottomed pans reduces the vibration significantly.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
